chart.cap_all_optimal: In this data every deductible step is cheapest somewhere – elsewhere only the highest and the lowest win.
chart.cap_never_optimal: Only the deductibles **{winners}** are ever the cheapest choice here; the faded steps {never} CHF are optimal at *no* level of healthcare costs.
chart.cap_no_tipping: The lowest deductible ({deductible} CHF) never pays off in the range shown.
chart.cap_red_line: The red line marks your expected healthcare costs ({amount} CHF); you can adjust the amount above. The cheapest deductible there is drawn in bold.
chart.cap_tipping: The grey dashed line is the tipping point\*\*: from **{tipping} CHF** the {low} CHF deductible pays off, below it the {other} CHF one. Between the best and the worst deductible lie up to {spread} CHF per year.

disclaimer.body:
From
the official premium data the app works out what the person described would pay at the
healthcare costs given – no more than that. Which insurance suits someone depends
on things that do not appear here:

- **Premium reductions**, supplementary insurance, the hospital contribution of
  CHF 15 per day, and the particulars of individual models.
- **Restrictions on the choice of doctor.** The alternative models are included in
  the premiums, but their conditions are not evaluated. The cheapest offer is not
  automatically the most suitable – the cheapest are almost always models that
  restrict the choice of doctor.
- **Children on different deductibles.** If children with the same insurer
  have different deductibles, the insurer sets the joint limit on their cost sharing
  itself (Art. 93 para. 3 KVV). That limit is not published, so the app calculates
  without it. With the same deductible for all the children, the statutory limit is
  included.
- **Higher coinsurance for some medicines.** If a medicine costs at least 10% more than the average of the cheapest third of products with the same active ingredient, coinsurance is 40% instead of 10%. The app uses 10% throughout.
- **Pregnancy.** From the 13th week of pregnancy until eight weeks after the birth, neither deductible nor coinsurance is charged (Art. 64 para. 7 KVG). The app still counts both.
- **The tipping point is exact to the franc, but the difference there is in
  centimes.** The direction it indicates – high or low deductible – is reliable, the
  precise amount is not.

What counts is what the insurers state and the official
[priminfo.admin.ch]({priminfo}). For a decision with consequences, advice from an
independent body is worth it.

footnote.data: \* Based on the FOPH's official data via [opendata.swiss]({opendata}). The environmental levy refund ({rebate_year} CHF per year) is already deducted from the premiums.
footnote.pharm: \*\*\* Pharmacy models are missing as a category of their own. The FOPH defines five model categories and priminfo.admin.ch offers all five – PHARM among them. Yet the {year} premium data contains not a single PHARM row anywhere in Switzerland. Pharmacy models do exist – PharMed, Favorit Medpharm, casamed pharm, KPTwin.win – but the FOPH files them under PRAXIS and FLEX. Filtering for PHARM on priminfo therefore hides precisely those models. This app only offers the categories that actually occur in the data.
footnote.tipping_point: \*\* I have watched this tipping point hold steady for years. A [published formula]({formula}) for the 300 and 2500 steps confirms it, but compares only those two steps. That the middle deductibles *never* pay off only shows up when every step is calculated – which is what this app does. In the data of recent years it has held every time; because premiums are set anew each year, it can change.

household.sibling_automatic: **The children are all cheapest with {insurer} anyway – the sibling discount applies there automatically.** With {insurer} – {tariff} on tariff tiers {tiers}, the {count} children cost {total} CHF together instead of {separate} CHF at the standard rate, {saving} CHF less. This is included above.
household.sibling_discount:
**One insurer for all the children saves {saving} CHF a year.**

- Each child with the cheapest provider for them, no discount: {separate} CHF
- All {count} children with {insurer} – {tariff}, tiers {tiers}: {total} CHF

K3, K4 and K5 apply only to children of the same family with the same insurer. Discount and free choice per child are therefore mutually exclusive. The cheaper variant is counted above.
household.sibling_not_worth: **One insurer for all the children does not pay here.** Each child on its own cheapest offer costs {separate} CHF in total; all the children with the same insurer cost at least {total} CHF (cheapest with {insurer}).
household.switch_note: “Switch” shows what you save a year by moving from today's contract to the recommendation in this table. With the current deductible given, that is the whole yearly cost – premiums, deductible and coinsurance at the expected healthcare costs; without it, only the difference in insurer and model, at the recommended deductible. “What changes” names only what is worth it: if another insurer or model adds less than {threshold} CHF, only the deductible is named. Children sharing one insurer are compared with the recommendation in the box above. Below {threshold} CHF of saving a year it says “no”.
household.unknown_tiers: The premium data carries the child tier(s) {tiers}, whose conditions are not known here. They are left out of the calculation – so the sibling discount could be larger than shown below.
lead:
You say what you expect to spend on doctors this year.

The app works out the rest – the insurer, model and deductible with the lowest total costs, for every person in the household and limited to the tariff models that suit you. Sibling discounts for several children are taken into account too. The calculation uses the official premium data for basic insurance\*.

total_costs_explainer:
**Total costs are premiums + deductible + coinsurance**, and so everything you pay yourself in a year. Of whatever lies above the deductible you pay {rate} yourself, but at most {cap_adult} CHF per year ({cap_child} CHF for children). Above that the insurer pays everything.

Looking only at the premium gets you nowhere: the lowest premium always carries the highest deductible. What pays off depends on how often you need a doctor. Of course you can't know that exactly. Base your estimate on what you spent in recent years, and add anything you can see coming – a planned operation, an ongoing therapy or regular medication.
